newsitem.title: INDIA: India minister presses for oil import duty cuts.
newsitem.headline: India minister presses for oil import duty cuts.

text.p: India's petroleum ministry on Tuesday pressed the case for cuts in import duties on crude oil as an alternative to increases in state-controlled petroleum product prices, national news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The government is under pressure to find a way of paying off its oil pool deficit -- money owed oil companies for selling products below market prices to subsidise consumers.
The deficit stood at 155 billion rupees at the end of 1996/97 (April-March).

"The prime concern of the ministry is to contain the deficit but we are not interested in hiking prices. The petroleum sector seeks reliefs from the Finance Ministry," junior Petroleum Minister T.R. Balu told PTI.

Finance Minister P.Chidambaram in an interview with Reuters Financial televison on Sunday said he was willing to consider various options to reduce the oil pool deficit, including cuts in import duties cuts so long as the shortfall in government revenues could be made up elsewhere.
Balu said import duties on crude should be abolished as it did not make any sense since government was the sole importer.
"Abolition of customs duties would result in a saving of over 45 billion rupees to the petroleum industry," he said.
He added that a similar abolition of excise levies on petroleum products would yield over 69 billion rupees.

Balu said the Finance Ministry enjoyed a windfall of an additional 42 billion rupees through extra custom duties revenues following the sudden escalation in the international prices of crude during 1996-97.
Balu said the finance ministry should find some way to return the money.
Last year's oil economy budget had assumed international crude prices of around $17 a barrel, but prices shot up to $24, and have since come back to around $19.60 for North Sea Brent.
The ministry sustains subsidies totalling 184.4 billion rupees for petroleum products such as diesel, kerosene, and liquified petroleum gas (LPG).
Balu also argued against the fertilisers industry receiving subsidies on petroleum product inputs amounting t15.7 billion rupees.
The subsidy on diesel was 83.4 billion rupees, on kerosene 63.5 billion and LPG 19.5 billion, he said.

Balu said he would discuss with the Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral various options for tackling the oil pool deficit shortly before the United Front steering committee takes up the issue for discussion on May 25.
Balu said it was too early to leave petroleum prices to market forces in India.
"It could be done in a gradual or phased manner only at a later stage without affecting the new industries coming up in the petroleum sector" he said.
